report_title: MuddyWater (G0069) Actor Intelligence Pack — Stage-1 CTI Extraction
source: MITRE ATT&CK G0069 (https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0069/); CISA/FBI/NSA/CNMF joint advisory AA22-055A (https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa22-055a); MENA-Threat-Actor-Tracker (iran-apt/apt-groups-iran.md, ksa-apt/apt-groups-ksa-high-confidence.md)

actor.name: MuddyWater
actor.attribution: Iran-nexus; subordinate element of Iran's Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS), per CISA/FBI/NSA joint advisory AA22-055A

key_campaigns.name: CISA/FBI/NSA/CNMF joint advisory AA22-055A
key_campaigns.summary: MOIS-attributed global campaign; documented MuddyWater TTPs, malware (PowGoop, Small Sieve, Mori, Canopy/STARWHALE, POWERSTATS) and IOCs.

key_campaigns.name: MuddyViper backdoor campaign vs. Israeli and Egyptian orgs
key_campaigns.summary: Backdoor campaign targeting Israeli and Egyptian organizations.

ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has performed credential dumping with Mimikatz and procdump64.exe.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — process access to lsass.exe and procdump command-line / Mimikatz signatures are highly observable in EDR and process-creation logs

ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has performed credential dumping with LaZagne.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — LaZagne execution and registry/LSA secret access are detectable via process and registry telemetry

ttps.technique_name: OS Credential Dumping: Cached Domain Credentials
ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has performed credential dumping with LaZagne.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — cached-credential access is subtler; best caught via LaZagne process/behavior signatures

ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has used malware to collect the victim's IP address and domain name.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — built-in recon commands (ipconfig) are common but suspicious in tight process-lineage context

ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has stored obfuscated JavaScript code in an image file named temp.jpg.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — payload hidden in image files leaves little log signal; better suited to hunting on temp.jpg-style artifacts and script-from-image patterns

ttps.technique_name: Obfuscated Files or Information: Compile After Delivery
ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has used the .NET csc.exe tool to compile executables from downloaded C# code.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — csc.exe spawned by script interpreters (mshta/powershell/wscript) is a strong, log-visible anomaly

ttps.technique_name: Obfuscated Files or Information: Command Obfuscation
ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has used Daniel Bohannon's Invoke-Obfuscation framework and obfuscated PowerShell scripts, plus Base64 obfuscation of VBScripts and PowerShell commands.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — obfuscated/encoded PowerShell is detectable via script-block logging and entropy/encoding heuristics

ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has used malware that can collect the victim's username.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — whoami/username enumeration is common; value is in process-lineage correlation

ttps.technique_name: Masquerading: Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location
ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has disguised malicious executables and used filenames and Registry key names associated with Windows Defender.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — Defender-themed filenames/registry keys in non-standard paths are detectable but require baselining

ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has used C2 infrastructure to receive exfiltrated data.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — exfil over C2 blends with C2 traffic; detectable via volume/beacon anomalies rather than discrete signatures

ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has used malware that leveraged WMI for execution and querying host information.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — WMI process creation and WMI-Activity operational logs provide strong telemetry

ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has used a PowerShell backdoor to check for Skype connections on the target machine.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — netstat-style checks are common; the Skype-connectivity check pattern is a distinctive hunt indicator

ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has used scheduled tasks to establish persistence.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — scheduled-task creation is logged (Event ID 4698 / Security-Task Scheduler) and highly detectable

ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has used malware to obtain a list of running processes on the system.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — tasklist/Get-Process enumeration is common but meaningful in process-lineage context

ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has used PowerShell for execution.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — script-block/module logging and suspicious PowerShell parenting are core, well-covered detections

ttps.technique_name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Windows Command Shell
ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has used a custom tool for creating reverse shells.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — cmd.exe reverse-shell patterns and anomalous parent processes are visible in process-creation logs

ttps.technique_name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Visual Basic
ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has used VBScript files to execute its POWERSTATS payload, as well as macros.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — wscript/cscript executing VBS, especially spawned by Office, is a strong detectable signal

ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has developed tools in Python including Out1.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — Python interpreter presence on Windows endpoints is unusual but under-instrumented; hunt candidate

ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has used JavaScript files to execute its POWERSTATS payload.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — JS executed via wscript/mshta, especially from Office lineage, is detectable in process logs

ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has used HTTP for C2 communications.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — HTTP C2 detectable via proxy/beacon analytics and JA3/URI anomalies, but blends with normal web traffic

ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has stored a decoy PDF file within a victim's %temp% folder.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — local staging in %temp% is common and noisy; better as a hunt over file-write telemetry

ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has used malware that can collect the victim's OS version and machine name.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — systeminfo-style discovery is common; suspicious mainly in process-lineage context

ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has used malware that checked if the ProgramData folder had folders or files with keywords 'Kasper,' 'Panda,' or 'ESET.'
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — the specific AV-vendor keyword enumeration is a distinctive behavioral pattern worth a targeted rule/hunt

ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has used cmd.exe net user /domain to enumerate domain users.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — 'net user /domain' and net group commands are directly observable in command-line logging

ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has used NordVPN to proxy phishing emails, making them appear to originate from France.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — commercial-VPN sender infrastructure is largely off-endpoint; hunt/enrichment candidate via email-header and geo analysis

ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has controlled POWERSTATS from behind a proxy network to obfuscate C2 location, used compromised websites that victims connected to randomly to relay information to C2, and used go-socks5 variants to bypass firewalls and NAT.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — external proxy relays via compromised sites are hard to distinguish at the endpoint; network/hunt candidate

ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has used web services including OneHub to distribute remote access tools.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — legitimate cloud/web services as C2 blend with normal traffic; hunt on proxy logs for anomalous file-sharing access

ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has used one C2 to obtain enumeration scripts and monitor web logs, but a different C2 to send data back.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — multi-stage channel separation is an architectural trait inferred from network analysis; hunt candidate

ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has used malware that can upload additional files to the victim's machine and used PowerShell commands to install remote management and monitoring (RMM) software on the victim's machine.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — PowerShell downloads (Invoke-WebRequest/DownloadFile) and unexpected RMM installers are strongly detectable

ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has used malware that can capture screenshots of the victim's machine.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — screen-capture APIs leave little discrete log signal; behavioral/EDR hunt candidate

ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has used tools to encode C2 communications including Base64 encoding.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — Base64-encoded C2 detectable via network content inspection and encoding heuristics where TLS is not used

ttps.technique_name: Office Application Startup: Office Template Macros
ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has used a Word Template, Normal.dotm, for persistence.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — modification of Normal.dotm / Word startup templates is a specific, detectable file-write persistence pattern

ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has decoded base64-encoded PowerShell, JavaScript, and VBScript.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — decode routines (FromBase64String, certutil -decode) are observable in script-block and command-line logging

ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has exploited the Microsoft Exchange memory corruption vulnerability (CVE-2020-0688).
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — Exchange exploitation detectable via web/IIS logs and post-exploit child processes of w3wp.exe

ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has exploited the Office vulnerability CVE-2017-0199 for execution.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — CVE-2017-0199 triggers Office spawning network/script children, a well-detected process-lineage anomaly

ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has distributed URLs in phishing e-mails that link to lure documents.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — malicious-link clicks detectable via email/URL gateway and proxy logs; endpoint signal is indirect

ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has attempted to get users to open malicious PDF attachments and to enable macros and launch malicious Microsoft Word documents, including a Word document with a malicious VBA macro.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — Office apps spawning script/child processes after macro enablement is a core detectable behavior

ttps.technique_name: User Execution: Malicious Copy and Paste
ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has leveraged ClickFix type tactics enticing victims to copy and paste malicious PowerShell code.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — ClickFix leaves PowerShell launched from explorer/RunMRU; detectable via command-line and RunMRU registry hunting

ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has exploited the Microsoft Netlogon vulnerability (CVE-2020-1472, Zerologon).
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — Zerologon exploitation is detectable via Netlogon (4742/5805) and DC event anomalies

ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has used CMSTP.exe and a malicious INF to execute its POWERSTATS payload.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — CMSTP.exe with an INF is a rare LOLBin pattern with very low false-positive rate

ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has used mshta.exe to execute its POWERSTATS payload and to pass a PowerShell one-liner for execution.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — mshta.exe spawning PowerShell / with remote or scripted args is a strong, well-covered LOLBin detection

ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has used malware that leveraged rundll32.exe in a Registry Run key to execute a .dll.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — rundll32 launching non-standard DLLs from Run keys is detectable via process + registry telemetry

ttps.technique_name: Remote Access Software: Remote Desktop Software
ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has leveraged RMM solutions including ScreenConnect, AteraAgent, SimpleHelp, Action1, Level, and PDQ to facilitate follow-on actions.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — unsanctioned RMM installs/execution are detectable via process, service, and known-binary/network signatures (a signature MuddyWater TTP)

ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has used a PowerShell backdoor to check for Skype connectivity on the target machine.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — the Skype-connectivity software check is a distinctive PowerShell behavior visible in script-block logs

ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has used malware to check running processes against a hard-coded list of security tools often used by malware researchers.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — AV/security-tool enumeration is a distinctive pattern detectable in script/command telemetry

ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has used compromised mailboxes within target organizations to send spearphishing emails.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — internal-origin phishing detectable via mail-flow anomalies and unusual send patterns from compromised accounts

ttps.technique_name: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder
ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has added Registry Run key HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run\SystemTextEncoding to establish persistence.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — Run-key creation (esp. the 'SystemTextEncoding' value) is directly detectable via registry-modification telemetry

ttps.technique_name: Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism: Bypass User Account Control
ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater uses various techniques to bypass UAC.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — known UAC-bypass patterns (fodhelper, eventvwr, etc.) are detectable but the source is generic; baselining needed

ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has run a tool that steals passwords saved in victim email.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — reading credential files leaves little discrete log signal; hunt candidate via file-access telemetry

ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has performed credential dumping with LaZagne and other tools, including by dumping passwords saved in victim email.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — credential-store access detectable mainly through known tool (LaZagne) execution signatures

ttps.technique_name: Credentials from Password Stores: Credentials from Web Browsers
ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has run tools including Browser64 to steal passwords saved in victim web browsers.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — access to browser credential stores (Login Data files) detectable via file-access and known-tool telemetry

ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has used malware that has the capability to execute malicious code via COM, DCOM, and Outlook.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — COM/DCOM abuse is under-instrumented and noisy; hunt candidate via DCOM lateral/execution telemetry

ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has used malware that can execute PowerShell scripts via DDE.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — DDE causing Office to spawn PowerShell is a strong, detectable process-lineage anomaly

ttps.technique_name: Archive Collected Data: Archive via Utility
ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has used the native Windows cabinet creation tool, makecab.exe, likely to compress stolen data.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — makecab.exe used outside servicing contexts is a detectable LOLBin staging pattern

ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has sent phishing emails to targets from the email address support@microsoftonlines[.]com.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — phishing detectable at email gateway via sender reputation and lookalike-domain analysis

ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has compromised third parties and used compromised accounts to send spearphishing emails with targeted attachments, including the attachment Cybersecurity.doc which served as the primary payload.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — attachment-based spearphishing detectable via mail sandboxing and macro-content analysis

ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has sent targeted spearphishing e-mails with malicious links.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — link-based spearphishing detectable via URL rewriting/detonation and proxy telemetry

ttps.technique_name: Exfiltration Over Web Service: Exfiltration to Cloud Storage
ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has attempted to exfiltrate data to Wasabi, a cloud storage service, using Rclone.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — Rclone process/command-line and connections to Wasabi/cloud-storage endpoints are detectable via process + network telemetry

ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has used ports 8043 and 8848 for botnet C2 communication.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — traffic to ports 8043/8848 is detectable via netflow/firewall analytics as a network-side indicator

ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has used AES to encrypt C2 responses.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — custom AES-encrypted C2 payloads defeat content inspection; hunt on beacon/traffic-shape anomalies

ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater maintains persistence on victim networks through side-loading DLLs to trick legitimate programs into running malware.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — DLL side-loading detectable via unsigned/anomalous module loads from unexpected paths (requires image-load telemetry)

ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has established domains, some of which appeared to spoof legitimate domains for use in operations.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — off-victim infrastructure acquisition is not endpoint-observable; intel/hunt candidate via registration and lookalike-domain monitoring

ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has used file sharing services including OneHub, Sync, and TeraBox to distribute tools.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — adversary use of legitimate file-sharing services is off-endpoint; hunt candidate via proxy access to these services

ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has used publicly available malware for operations, likely to blend in with other cybercriminals.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — capability acquisition is not directly observable in victim telemetry; intelligence/hunt candidate

ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has used legitimate tools ConnectWise, RemoteUtilities, and SimpleHelp to gain access to the target environment.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — tool acquisition itself is off-endpoint; downstream use maps to T1219.002 which is detectable — this entry is a hunt/intel candidate

ttps.technique_name: Gather Victim Network Information: Network Topology
ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has mapped target networks; access to this information and more is then shared/sold to other Iran threat actors.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — external recon and access-brokering are not endpoint-observable; strategic intel/hunt candidate

ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater has used support@microsoftonlines[.]com to send phishing emails masquerading as Microsoft security updates, and has impersonated TMCell (Altyn Asyr CJSC), the primary mobile operator in Turkmenistan.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — impersonation is a lure/branding trait best countered via email lookalike-brand analysis and user awareness; hunt candidate

ttps.procedure_description: MuddyWater can disable the system's local proxy settings.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — changes to proxy settings (ProxyEnable/ProxyServer registry values) are detectable via registry-modification telemetry

detection_signals: mshta.exe or cmstp.exe spawning powershell.exe / executing INF or remote scripts
csc.exe spawned by a script interpreter (compile-after-delivery)
Office application (winword.exe/excel.exe) spawning powershell/wscript/cscript/cmd child processes
Registry Run key value 'SystemTextEncoding' under HKCU...\CurrentVersion\Run
'net user /domain' and net group domain enumeration in command-line logs
Scheduled task creation (Event ID 4698) with script/LOLBin actions
procdump against lsass.exe or Mimikatz process-access to lsass
Unsanctioned RMM binary install/execution (ScreenConnect, AteraAgent, SimpleHelp, Action1, Level, PDQ)
PowerShell script-block logs containing Invoke-Obfuscation / Base64 / FromBase64String / Skype-connectivity or AV-keyword checks
Rclone execution or outbound connections to Wasabi/cloud-storage endpoints
Outbound C2 to non-standard ports 8043 and 8848
Registry proxy-setting changes (ProxyEnable/ProxyServer) disabling local proxy
notes: All 68 seed ATT&CK techniques preserved and enriched with MuddyWater-specific procedure descriptions, observed tooling, a detection_feasibility hint (the field decision-agent routes on), and source citations. Attribution to Iran/MOIS is high-confidence per CISA/FBI/NSA AA22-055A and corroborated by the MENA-Threat-Actor-Tracker high-confidence tiering. IOCs are deliberately minimal and conservatively sourced: the microsoftonlines[.]com domain, support@microsoftonlines[.]com sender, and non-standard C2 ports 8043/8848 are the only indicators attributable to authoritative public reporting (MITRE G0069 / AA22-055A) in this pass. No file hashes or C2 IPs are included because they could not be responsibly attributed to a fetched primary source here (CISA AA22-055A returned HTTP 403 to automated fetch; its indicator list should be ingested directly from the advisory PDF/appendix before hashes/IPs are added). Tactic labels were normalized to single canonical ATT&CK tactics for decision-agent routing (seed multi-tactic strings collapsed, e.g. T1053.005 -> persistence, T1574.001 -> persistence, T1684.001 -> resource-development per current ATT&CK). Low detection-feasibility techniques (hunt candidates rather than detection candidates): T1027.003, T1059.006, T1074.001, T1090, T1090.002, T1102.002, T1104, T1113, T1552.001, T1559.001, T1573.001, T1583.001, T1583.006, T1588.001, T1588.002, T1590.004, T1684.001.
